source.title: Linearly Decoding Refused Knowledge in Aligned Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study reports how often two jailbreak-prompt methods elicit responses from instruction-tuned models that initially refuse some questions. This conceptually tests whether jailbreaks bypass refusal, but it does not test compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
record.gate_note: The study's probe results concern whether refused numerical information is decodable from hidden states, not per-token KL, localization in a small parameter set, or the cause or depth of safety training. The reported refusal-rate table is not a fine-tuning experiment. Table 2 reports additional AIM attack-success rates by model and attribute; selected cells are recorded below, and the other cells are noted under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study uses two jailbreak prompts, a five-shot ICL prompt and the AIM role-play persona, as a tool to obtain labels for linear probes. Its findings concern whether refused numerical attributes are decodable from hidden states. It does no fine-tuning, per-token KL analysis, prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, parameter localization or deepening training. The attack-success rates in Appendix B.1 are incidental to obtaining labels. They come from persona and in-context prompts, not from getting past the response opening, so they do not measure what V4 names. Many refused questions (e.g., a fictional person's height) are refused on uncertainty grounds rather than harm. The paper mentions shallow alignment only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that instruction-tuned models keep linearly decodable representations of refused content. Base-model probes sometimes transfer to instruction-tuned models, and probe predictions correlate with pairwise comparisons. They argue instruction-tuning alters surface behaviour rather than underlying representations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses prompt-based jailbreaks and hidden-state probing, not fine-tuning examples, per-token KL analysis, or methods for deepening safety.
record.method_sensitivity: Jailbreak method and model affect attack success: ICL is reported as perfect across tested attributes and models; AIM varies by attribute and model. Probe performance also varies by entity type and jailbreak prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: Five-shot ICL jailbreaks reached 1.0 success on initially refused numerical questions in gemma-2-9b/2b-it and Yi-6B-Chat. AIM role-play averaged 0.809, ranging from 0.651 (gemma-2-2b-it) to 0.914 (gemma-2-9b-it) and varying strongly by attribute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-level jailbreaks (in-context demonstrations, persona role-play) bypass refusal in small instruction-tuned models at model- and topic-dependent rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Refused numerical attributes are linearly decodable from innocuous hidden states. Probes trained on base models sometimes transfer to instruct models, and probe predictions correlate with pairwise-comparison rankings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction tuning suppresses expression of refused information without removing its linear representation.

record.problems: The study covers a limited set of relatively small models, four entity types, and two jailbreak prompts. It uses greedily decoded responses as probe labels, and the authors note that results may vary with different prompts and labels. Many probing results are presented in plots; the study does not report uncertainty estimates for the attack-success rates.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports many additional AIM attack-success rates by entity type, attribute, and model. They are omitted here to keep the extraction selective; the table includes further conditions beyond the AIM cells recorded above. The remaining per-attribute probing and base-to-instruction probe-transfer plots are not extracted as claim-version results because they do not test the listed versions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the attack-success rows to V4 and labelled them. That is unsupported: the jailbreaks are persona and ICL prompts, not opening-token attacks, and they serve only to generate probe labels. Refusal-rate Table 1 shows that many refused questions are benign but uncertain, such as a fictional person's height. The study is not one of V4's original sources, but it does not test V4. No verdicts are given.
